method.check_1: Confirm official/DOI identity, publisher, title, and existence.
method.check_2: Inspect the exact table, abstract, section, or data field; preserve year, geography, unit, boundary, range, and scenario.
method.check_3: Corroborate interpretation independently, reproduce arithmetic, or explicitly test for boundary and double-counting errors.

checks.evidence: USGS publication page and DOI 10.3133/cir1441 identify the national 2015 inventory.
Abstract and Table 1 report 322 Bgal/d total and 281 Bgal/d freshwater withdrawals.
Category/source components and historical tables were reconciled; the 0.7 Bgal/d fresh-source difference is retained as rounding, and the date is labeled 2015.
Circular 1441 and Professional Paper 1894-D are official USGS products with explicit definitions.
2015 estimates show thermoelectric consumption 4.31 of 133 Bgal/d total withdrawal versus irrigation consumption 73.2 of 118 Bgal/d.
PP1894-D independently models the same contrast: 4 percent freshwater thermoelectric versus 72 percent crop-irrigation consumptive fractions for 2010–20.
USGS PP1894-D page and DOI 10.3133/pp1894D resolve to the 2010–20 national model.
Tables 1–3 report 105,497/75,698, 35,440/4,219, and 82,656/2,904 Mgal/d withdrawal/consumption averages.
The three-sector arithmetic was recomputed to 223,593 Mgal/d withdrawal and 82,821 Mgal/d consumption, and the package forbids calling these all-sector totals.
USGS Circular 1441 domestic section and EPA WaterSense official program page were verified.
USGS reports 26.6 Bgal/d total, 23.3 public deliveries, 3.26 self-supplied, and 82 gpcd.
23.3 + 3.26 = 26.56 Bgal/d, consistent with the rounded 26.6; EPA independently repeats the 82 gpcd national household reference.
USGS PP1894-D is the primary 2010–20 consumptive-use source.
Table 1 reports crop irrigation 105,497 Mgal/d withdrawal and 75,698 Mgal/d consumption, rounded to 72 percent.
75,698 divided by 105,497 reproduces 71.75 percent; Circular 1441 independently reports high 2015 irrigation consumption.
USGS industrial-water page and Circular 1441 identify the 2015 self-supplied industrial category.
The official summary reports 14.8 Bgal/d total, 14.0 freshwater, and 82 percent surface water.
USGS documentation states public-supply industrial deliveries have not been estimated nationally since 1995; the claim explicitly preserves the omission.
Census NAICS pages establish distinct resin (325211) and downstream plastics/rubber product (326) boundaries; NIST and DOI sources exist.
USGS industrial data are not plastics-specific and exclude public deliveries; the historical EPA survey combines organic chemicals, plastics, and synthetic fibers.
NIST review documents data gaps and the 2023 cross-database study finds divergent water results for identical resins, invalidating a universal coefficient.
LBNL 2024 report DOI 10.71468/P1WC7Q and LBNL 2026 analysis page were verified.
Sources report 66 billion liters in 2023 and 0.14–0.28 billion m3 in 2028.
Conversions reproduce 47.77 Mgal/d for 2023 and 101.3–202.7 Mgal/d for 2028; projection status is explicit.
LBNL defines direct facility and indirect electricity water; USGS separately accounts for thermoelectric water.
The LBNL indirect estimate is attributed to electricity generation rather than a second direct facility withdrawal.
A national sum including both full power-sector water and data-center allocated electricity water counts the same upstream flow twice; validator requires separate display.
USGS 2026 official release and NWAA data catalog exist and identify the assessment.
Release reports nearly 27 million people, about 8 percent, and roughly 80,000 watersheds for 2009–20.
Method scope was checked against the data catalog; claim is constrained to demand versus modeled natural supply and not converted to utility failure.
USGS coastal synthesis DOI 10.1007/s10040-009-0514-3, Miami SIR, and NCA5 water chapter were verified.
Sources identify lateral, vertical, and well pathways and control by pumping/hydraulic conditions, with sea-level rise as an aggravating driver.
Contrasting Miami, Long Island, and Brunswick evidence confirms consequences range from managed interfaces to local closures and existing plumes, so no universal date is defensible.
Miami-Dade official vulnerability page, county model memorandum, and USGS SIR were verified.
County model memorandum states evaluated wellfields are not impacted through 2040 even under the high sea-level-rise case.
USGS independently confirms ongoing intrusion controls; package preserves the 2040 model horizon and refuses both a run-out claim and post-2040 extrapolation.
Bureau of Reclamation post-2026 official process page was verified.
The process page establishes expiration of current guidelines and need for water-year 2027 operations; January 2026 draft EIS had no preferred alternative.
The regulatory date was checked against Reclamation process milestones and is encoded as governance, not hydrologic exhaustion.
TWDB official 2027 State Water Plan page and adopted plan record were verified.
Plan reports potential shortages of 3.6 million acre-feet in 2030 and 5.8 million in 2080 under drought-of-record planning conditions.
Plan's thousands of recommended strategies show the numbers are no-action planning counterfactuals; dashboard language preserves that condition.
New Mexico Office of the State Engineer official rulemaking record and technical planning materials were verified.
Planning record uses approximately 25 percent less river/aquifer water and a roughly 750,000 acre-foot gap over 50 years.
NCA5 independently supports Southwest runoff/groundwater and demand risks; the state values remain labeled planning estimates rather than observations.
USGS SIR 2023-5143 and Agricultural Water Management DOI 10.1016/j.agwat.2020.106061 were verified.
USGS reports 286.4 million acre-feet decline and 2.91 billion remaining recoverable storage in 2019; model reports 24 percent affected irrigated area by 2100.
Storage decline and agricultural-viability model were kept as different metrics; large remaining regional storage prevents an aquifer-empty interpretation.
DOE/USGS technology pages and official Carlsbad, Tampa, El Paso, and California sources were verified.
Operating profiles report 50, 25, and 27.5 Mgal/d capacities and different intake/concentrate arrangements.
California strategy independently catalogs energy, brine, environmental, permitting, cost, and equity constraints, supporting site-specific rather than universal viability.
Peer-reviewed LBNL/Desalination DOI source and USGS 2015 domestic-use inventory were verified.
Source interval is 3.2–4.5 kWh/m3 and domestic use is 26.6 Bgal/d.
Independent unit calculation converts 26.6 Bgal/d to annual cubic meters and produces 117.6–165.4 TWh/year; exclusions are explicit.
EPA 2019 brief, Nature DOI 10.1038/s41586-021-03900-w, ENERGY STAR criteria, and WHO quantity guidance were verified.
EPA capacities, Nature 5 L drinking target, WHO 5.3/20 L references, and USGS/EPA 82 gpcd full-use reference were kept distinct.
Capacity and energy proxy calculations show a 10,000 L/day unit supports about 1,887 drinking-only person-equivalents but only 32 full U.S.-use equivalents; proxy is labeled non-certified.
EPA technical brief and 2024 EPA research record were verified.
EPA reports microbial growth/contaminant pathways and real-world heterotrophic bacteria with opportunistic-pathogen evidence.
Both technology guidance and empirical field evidence require treatment/disinfection and ongoing maintenance; no raw-condensate safety claim is retained.
